item.title: Romantic Hypocrisy: Perceiving and Practicing Infidelity
item.description:
Infidelity

Romantic Hypocrisy: Perceiving and Practicing Infidelity

The behaviors partners both condemn and commit.

Posted October 22, 2026

Key points
  • People judge the behavior of others more severely than their own behavior, exhibiting actor-observer bias.
  • There is a tendency to downplay one's own behavior but not that of others.
  • Partners view sexual behavior differently when the intent is ambiguous.

Infidelity is a significant threat within exclusive romantic relationships that, in many cases, can lead to dissolution. But how do you define it? Most couples would agree there are definite examples of cheating, and then there is the grey area. Text messages, browsing singles websites, and expressing interest in (attractive) others are examples of behaviors that might be viewed as ambiguous in terms of interest and intent. The significance of interpretation is important within romantic relationships, considering the potential for misunderstanding. Research explains.

Source: Image by Sunrise from Pixabay

Romantic Hypocrisy

Researchers Ashley E. Thompson and Lucia F. O’Sullivan examined the way partners engage in inconsistent explanations of infidelity in a piece aptly entitled “I Can But You Can’t.”[i] Using online surveys with 810 adult participants, they compared opinions about infidelity given by participants regarding their own behavior and the behavior of their partners. People judged their own behavior more permissively than the way they viewed the behavior of their partners, yet only in certain areas. They were more permissive in the areas of emotional/affectionate and technology/online behaviors, but not when viewing behavior that was categorized as sexual/explicit or solitary.

Many study participants admitted to being unfaithful, especially within the categories of emotional/affectionate and technology/online. Thompson and O’Sullivan explored some of the reasons behind the differences in the ways partners viewed the same behavior—depending on who committed it. They note that generally, individuals tend to judge the behavior of others more severely than their own, a tendency known as actor-observer bias. This self-serving bias blames others and attributes one’s own bad behavior to external factors, situational or contextual, yet attributes the bad behavior of others to internal reasons, such as stable personal or dispositional characteristics. They give the example of someone blaming one’s own low exam score on the situational factor of a poor instructor, while explaining someone else’s low score on a dispositional factor such as low intelligence.

Inconsistencies in Judgments and Behaviour

Within romantic relationships, Thompson and O’Sullivan found that individuals classify certain behaviors as infidelity and then report participating in them themselves. Their study included a sample of 810 individuals, 328 men and 482 women, with a mean age of 34.4 years. Most of them lived in the United States, almost 90% were heterosexual, and most were in a committed relationship.

The measures included four subscales. The Sexual/Explicit Behaviour subscale included explicit physical contact such as oral sex and sexual intercourse. The Technology/Online Behaviour subscale related to explicit technology-facilitated communication, including messaging, browsing a singles website, and webcam masturbation. The Romantic/Affectionate Behaviour subscale included displaying romantic interest or intimate activities, including sharing secrets, having a casual dinner, and providing emotional support. The Solitary Behaviour subscale covered behaviors people typically do alone, such as masturbating or viewing pornography.

Detecting Double Standards

Regarding areas of inconsistency, Thompson and O’Sullivan reported that differences in judgments between self and others revealed a self-enhancing bias and greater willingness to downplay one’s own negative behavior, especially when it was more ambiguous, in order to maintain a positive self-image. They found this actor-observer difference in judgments of technology/online and emotional/affectionate infidelity behaviors, not solitary or sexual/explicit behaviors.

Regarding solitary behaviors, Thompson and O’Sullivan noted that a substantial number of participants viewed them as suggestive of infidelity to some extent because they involved arousal or attraction to someone else, but did not view them as serious violations of monogamy expectations. Yet as a practical matter, a significant number of partners would view them as distasteful and undesirable, perhaps even to the extent they would rethink a relationship.

This research highlights the importance of discussing fidelity expectations early on in a relationship to avoid misunderstanding and prevent incompatible pairings. Healthy, sustainable, long-term relationships start with good communication and are sustained through mutual respect, love, and commitment.

item.title: Can Forgiving Someone Who Hurt You Make You Healthier?
item.description:
Forgiveness

Can Forgiving Someone Who Hurt You Make You Healthier?

Why releasing resentment isn't absolution but a path to healing and a happy life.

Posted October 22, 2026

Key points
  • Forgiveness can reduce depression and anxiety and may even be associated with greater longevity.
  • Lingering resentment can prolong the body's stress response, potentially affecting immunity.
  • Some wounds are too deep to forgive, but releasing self-blame can be a powerful path to healing.

Forgiveness as a concept can be incendiary and polarizing.

Some view forgiveness as surrender, a form of exonerating an abuser and accepting bad behavior. They see it as a shrugging of the shoulders and giving someone who has hurt them deeply a free pass.

Yet others view it as anything but. They see it as liberation, a way to free themselves from the hold of someone who has caused them harm, a path to moving on.

At its core, forgiveness is about releasing your resentment over a past hurt and giving yourself permission to move from a place of pain to a life where you can flourish without being weighed down by an injustice. It is like removing a proverbial backpack that has been weighing you down. It’s a mindset that releases you from being chained to the past and to the event that harmed you.

Of course, some wounds are too deep, some acts too horrific, to forgive the person who inflicted them. That choice deserves respect. But there is another form of forgiveness that can be restorative: forgiving ourselves.

When we have been deeply hurt, at times we turn the blame inward. We ask, Could I have prevented what happened? Self-forgiveness means accepting the event was beyond our control and that we cannot alter the past. It releases blame that was never ours to bear, and extends to ourselves the compassion we might readily offer others.

After all, forgiveness is not about what we owe another person. It's a choice we make for ourselves. We forgive so that the experience does not take up precious space in the story of our life.

Whatever our personal view of forgiveness, science offers a compelling reason to consider it. In addition to reclaiming our peace, research suggests that letting go of resentment can benefit our mental and physical health and may even be associated with greater longevity.

Forgiveness is not absolution

It’s important to recognize that forgiveness is not absolution. People often get stuck in confusing the two. It is not saying that what happened to you is OK. Forgiveness does not ask us to condone past harm, excuse the inexcusable, or give someone who has hurt us deeply a free pass. At the heart of forgiveness is reclaiming our own peace, and because we deserve a future unencumbered by old stories that tether us to sorrow.

Nelson Mandela, South Africa’s first Black president, modeled this understanding after spending 27 years in prison. As he was known to have said as he walked out of the prison gate, it was essential that he leave his bitterness and hatred behind, or he would still be in prison—doing so was essential to his freedom.

Health benefits of embracing forgiveness

There is a compelling incentive to embrace forgiveness: profound health benefits. Science now shouts what sages have long whispered: It's important to let go. Holding on to anger can prolong our stress response.

We all know that emotional pain can leave its imprint on the body. Haven't we all felt the physical ache caused by an emotional wound? Doesn't the word heartache aptly capture the connection between emotional and physical suffering?

Science suggests this connection is more than a metaphor. An fMRI study found that social rejection activates brain regions that are also involved in processing physical pain. This helps explain why being rejected can hurt so deeply, even when no physical injury has occurred. The pain is emotional, but the body's response can be very real.

But the impact of emotional wounds doesn't end there. When hurt gives way to lingering anger and resentment, it can prolong the body's stress response, affecting cortisol levels. Chronically elevated cortisol can impair immunity and disrupt sleep, while prolonged stress may contribute to accelerated biological aging. This brings to mind the ancient Buddhist metaphor of clutching a burning coal, hoping to hurl it at someone who has wronged us, only to discover that we are the ones being burned. So it is with resentment. By holding tightly to the memory of being wronged, we prolong our own suffering.

But what happens when we hold on to that burning coal for years? Could forgiveness have implications not only for our health but also for our longevity?

In a study of more than 1,200 older adults, researchers found that those who made forgiveness conditional on an apology or a promise not to repeat the harm had a higher risk of dying during the three-year study. While this is not evidence that forgiveness extends life, it raises a compelling possibility. Holding on to resentment while waiting for someone else to make amends may take a toll on our physical health.

But there is clear evidence of forgiveness benefiting our mental health. Research suggests that forgiveness can reduce depression and anxiety. In one study of nearly 4,600 adults across five counties, those who participated in a brief forgiveness intervention experienced reductions in symptoms of both. And there are even greater benefits. Research suggests that practicing forgiveness can improve self-esteem and is associated with greater life satisfaction.

Ultimately, if our goal is to live a healthier, happier life, unencumbered by old burdens that tether us to sorrow, forgiveness offers an important pathway forward. It's a powerful way to reclaim our peace and refuse to let the past define our present.

As I have grappled with forgiveness in my own life, two extraordinary resources have deeply inspired me: the International Forgiveness Institute, which offers science-based strategies for letting go of resentment, and The Forgiveness Project, offering a moving collection of personal stories that illuminate the power of forgiveness to foster healing.

Perhaps the greatest gift of forgiveness is this: It has the power to transform a wound from a source of pain into a catalyst for growth. As the poet Rumi reminds us, “The wound is the place where the light enters you.”

item.title: The Beauty of Limitations
item.description:
Beauty

The Beauty of Limitations

How the fleeting nature of time makes it precious.

Posted October 22, 2026

Key points
  • Scarcity makes everything desirable.
  • Impermanence makes it possible for beauty to exist.
  • Knowing that a moment won’t last allow us to cherish it more fully.
Source: Image by Qogwarp from Pixabay

Scarcity is a pervasive condition of human existence. Everyday circumstances of limited resources (money and time) can make individuals experience a sense of scarcity. Their scarcity functions like an obstacle to goal pursuit, which intensifies the value of goal.

Scarcity prioritizes our choices and it can make us more effective. The time pressure of a deadline focuses our attention on using what we have most effectively. Distractions are less tempting. When we have little time left, we try to get more out of every moment. For example, we are more frugal with the toothpaste as the tube starts to run empty, and college seniors tend to get the most out of their time before graduation.

Scarcity makes everything more desirable. We will enjoy our lunch more for being deprived of breakfast—literally, hunger is the best sauce. Sometimes people want things precisely because they cannot have them: “The grass is always greener on the other side of the fence." Playing hard to get is a most effective strategy for attracting a partner, especially in the context of long-term love, in which a person wishes to be sure of their partner’s commitment. A “hard to get” player likes to appear busy, create intrigue, and keep their suitors guessing.

Scarcity also contributes to an interesting and a meaningful life. A life without limits would lose the beauty of its moments and become boring. Abundant time destroys the urgency for anything and need for quick action. Research shows that reminding individuals of the reality of death increases the value of life. Death represents life’s scarcity, which may influence subsequent efforts to protect the threatening aspects of death.

Midlife often heightens the feeling that there is not enough time left in life to waste. We overcome the illusion that we can be anything, do anything, and experience everything. We restructure our lives around the needs that are essential. This means that we accept that there will be many things we won’t do in our lives. Overcoming a midlife crisis requires accepting that life is finite (Strenger, 2011).

Like scarcity, impermanence refers to the concept of limitation. There is a beauty in impermanence. Knowing that a moment won’t last allows us to cherish it more fully. In fact, beauty is heightened by the very fact that it cannot last. Cherry blossoms, mist, rain, snow, autumn leaves, and other fleeting materials or phenomena especially signify aging and transience.

Impermanence is core to Japanese culture (Juniper, 2003). The concept of wabi-sabi, central to Japanese aesthetics, embraces the transient and imperfect nature of life, emphasizing simplicity, humility and the beauty found in natural flaws and impermanence. In this context, the concept of impermanence highlights the transient nature of all things. When many Japanese speak of beauty, they link it directly to the transience of all things: An object that lasts forever has far less aesthetic appeal than something fragile and short-lived.

This worldview frames impermanence not as a limitation but as a source of aesthetic. It offers a framework in which change is not feared but embraced, allowing impermanence to inspire wonder, reflection and a deeper connection to life’s fleeting moments. Impermanence, in that sense, makes it possible for beauty to exist.

item.title: Tired of Swiping? What Evolution Suggests Instead
item.description:
Mating

Tired of Swiping? What Evolution Suggests Instead

Who feels dating app exhaustion most, and what could help.

Posted October 22, 2026

Key points
  • Men and women report different frustrations with dating apps.
  • The apps do work well for some people, including many lesbian, gay, and bisexual users.
  • Repeated in-person contact builds familiarity, which may suit our psychology better than endless swiping.
Source: Image Image by NoName_13 from Pixabay

In my last post, I explored why dating apps leave many people exhausted, pointing to a mismatch between our evolved minds and endless choice. Here, I look at who feels that exhaustion most, who the apps still serve well, why run clubs (or any club, really) may feel different, and what an exhausted dater can do.

Men and women are not having the same experience

Dating exhaustion is not the same for everyone. Take, for example, the results from a 2022 Pew Research Center survey of 6,034 people in the USA. Of those who had used a dating site or app in the past year, about 54% of women felt overwhelmed by the number of messages they received, compared with 25% of men, while 64% of men felt insecure about receiving too few messages, compared with 40% of women. Among everyone who had ever dated online, women were also less likely than men to describe their experiences as positive (48% versus 57%).

These differences fit an evolutionary view. One of the core tenets of the field is that the sex investing more in offspring becomes a limiting resource, courted by the other sex and choosier about whom it accepts (Trivers, 1972); in humans, this logic has been used to explain why women tend to be the choosier sex. An app that gives many women a flood of interest and many men a trickle may simply magnify an asymmetry already present.

There is a competitive side, too. Much of my own research concerns intrasexual competition, meaning competition with members of one’s own sex for mates. In one early study, I found that women rated other women’s faces as less attractive when they were near peak fertility, while their ratings of men’s faces did not change (Fisher, 2004). Apps make the competition feel ever-present, given that every profile you admire is presumably being admired by others as well. I would predict that the sense of a crowded field adds to the exhaustion, but this idea needs proper testing.

Who the apps may work for

None of these findings means the apps are failing everyone. By 2017, meeting online had become the most common way heterosexual couples in the USA met, accounting for an estimated 39% of couples (Rosenfeld et al., 2019). In Pew’s 2022 survey, about one in 10 partnered adults had met their partner online, rising to about one in five among those under 30 and about one in four among lesbian, gay, and bisexual adults. LGB users were also more likely than straight users to describe their experiences as positive (61% versus 53%). For people whose local pool of potential partners is small, a wider net may be helpful.

Source: Image by ahmetyuksek from Pixabay

Why run clubs feel different

I recently spent a month in Chile as part of a partnership-building grant. While I was there, everyone in the university labs I interacted with seemed to have taken up running. Many group members were running long distances or even running marathons. Truthfully, I was surprised. They were all using Strava, the fitness-tracking app, which reported a 59% increase in running clubs on its platform in 2024. In Strava's own survey of more than 5,000 active people, more than half of Gen Z respondents said social connection was their main reason for joining a fitness group, and four times as many respondents preferred to meet new people through a fitness group than at a bar. My experiences in Chile certainly point to this change.

But why are we turning to fitness groups when we want to meet new people? A group or club shrinks the pool of new people to a number of faces you can actually come to know, and it provides repeated exposure, which tends to build liking. In a classic study, Moreland and Beach (1992) had four women of similar appearance attend a large college course 0, 5, 10, or 15 times without interacting with anyone. At the end of the term, students reported greater attraction to the women who had attended more often and saw them as more similar to themselves. The attraction measured was not specifically romantic, and those women never spoke to anyone, whereas a run club involves real conversation, but the study shows how much familiarity alone can do.

Shared activities also reveal what a profile cannot, such as how someone treats other people, copes with a hard hill, or makes a group laugh. Joel and colleagues’ work suggests that compatibility tends to show itself only once people meet. Whether run clubs actually produce more lasting relationships than apps do is, as yet, unknown, but I suspect the answer is “yes.”

Tips for dating now

What, then, should an exhausted dater do? I must note that none of the following has been tested per se, but each stems from the research I have described here and in my last post.

  1. Looking at fewer profiles in a sitting works with, rather than against, a mind that grows more rejecting as options pile up.
  2. Taking a moment to judge each profile deliberately, instead of on gut feel, may help protect how you see yourself.
  3. Before you open an app, decide on two or three qualities that matter most to you. Choice overload is more likely when people are unsure of their preferences, and knowing what you are looking for makes a long list of options easier to manage. (Side note: I truly think making an actual list of ‘wants’ and ‘needs’ is useful for this reason.)
  4. Read, and do not just look at the photos. With many options, people tend to fall back on traits they can judge at a glance and pay less attention to those that take longer to assess. Pausing over the bio or what someone have written is a small way to push back against that shortcut.
  5. Meet sooner rather than screening longer. Chemistry between two people is hard to predict before they meet, so a short, low-stakes coffee date may tell you more than another evening of studying profiles.
  6. Take breaks, and notice how the apps make you feel. Research suggests that exhaustion and a sense that one’s efforts are not paying off both grew over 12 weeks of app use, and more so among users with higher levels of depression, anxiety, or loneliness. If swiping consistently leaves you feeling worse, stepping away, or leaning on friends and other support, may be a better response rather than giving up.
  7. Turning up week after week to the same class, club, or volunteer group gives familiarity time to do its quiet work. (If you do not want to join a dating app at all, this tip is a real option for you.)

item.title: The Pleasure of Almost
item.description:
Motivation

The Pleasure of Almost

What if I don't actually want to get what I want?

Posted October 22, 2026

My alarm goes off. I stumble out of bed to check my email. Before coffee!

I check my email because I am waiting for people to get back to me. I am waiting to hear back from publishers. I am waiting to hear back from television production companies. I am waiting to hear back from poetry contests. I am waiting to hear back from people who said they would get back to me, some of whom seemed quite excited about getting back to me as soon as humanly possible.

What I want is an answer. And I want that answer to be a "yes." I have been very clear with the universe about this. But lately I’ve begun to suspect I don’t want all those yeses quite the way I had thought I did.

Peter Rollins
Source: Used with permission/Peter Rollins

Hunting the Rabbit

I recently spoke with Irish philosopher Peter Rollins on my podcast Fifty Words for Snow, where my cohost and I discuss words without English equivalents. Peter suggested something that sounded insane: that there may actually be pleasure in not getting what I want.

The word Peter brought us was jouissance. In psychoanalysis, jouissance refers to enjoyment that involves frustration, discomfort, or even suffering—the sort of thing that makes you continue doing something you claim you would very much like to stop doing. We imagine satisfaction waits at the end of our pursuit. But wanting itself gives us something: anticipation, purpose, a reason to get up and see whether anyone has emailed.

Peter used an example from philosopher Blaise Pascal: Imagine you are going hunting. You rise before dawn, lace your boots, pack a lunch. You know where the rabbits cross. Today, you might catch one. Then someone pulls up and hands you a rabbit. Here, they say. Saved you the trouble.

If the rabbit were all you wanted, this would be excellent service. You could go home. But something has been taken from you along with the trouble: the morning ahead, the listening, the possibility of movement in the grass.

Of course, if someone told you there were no rabbits anywhere in the woods, that would ruin the morning too. You need a rabbit. And you need it some distance away.

A Modest Lead

For years, I have hunted the Great Yes: A publisher saying yes. A producer saying yes. Someone with the authority to confirm that all this effort is leading somewhere.

Occasionally, I have caught it. I have published books and written for television shows. I know the pleasure of getting the call. But then the job ends. The book gets published. And then I need another “yes,” another rabbit.

I mean, I do want the book deal. If a publisher is reading this, please don’t interpret my growing self-awareness as a withdrawal of my submission. But I’m beginning to suspect that part of what I want is the pursuit: finding tracks, losing the tracks, finding them again. I like the hope, the anticipation. I like believing something could happen overnight. The trouble comes when I spend the entire morning staring at an empty clearing. When I check my email twenty times. Before breakfast.

But lately I’ve begun to notice that, alongside the frustration, it’s true: There’s something I enjoy about the whole thing. The calculating. The maneuvering. The anticipation and avoidance of obstacles. The possibility that today I’ll spot the ears of that elusive “yes” just above the grass.

Recognizing that part of me enjoys the pursuit seems to make the desire less onerous. I still want to catch the rabbit. But I can recognize that I have the privilege of being on a hunt, of having something I want to follow.

At any moment, something might move in the brush.

item.title: Halloween and Queer Spirituality
item.description:
Spirituality

Halloween and Queer Spirituality

Celebrating Halloween can help queer people embrace their sacredness.

Posted October 22, 2026

Key points
  • While mainstream religions tend to be hostile to queer people, Halloween can provide a sacred space for them.
  • The meaning of Halloween resonates deeply with queer people's experiences of living in the in-between.
  • Halloween can provide a space of belonging as it celebrates being an "outsider" and living on the edge.
  • Honouring queer lineage is a profound way to embrace queer sacredness.
Source: VladOrlov / iStock

Many religions attack queer people every day by calling us an abomination, a disease, or a sin. It is not a surprise that many queer people grow up to fear religions. For many, being queer means they have to leave their faith behind because it was a place of condemnation rather than comfort. It can create an empty spiritual space that is often hard to fill. However, for queer people who wish to have a spiritual life, our longing for meaning, ritual and connection rarely disappears.

For a growing number of queer people, Halloween, or Samhain (pronounced "sow-in") as many spiritual practitioners still call it, has become one of the places where they can find a spiritual home.

The sacred threshold

Samhain was, above all, a festival of thresholds. It represents the end of harvest into the winter, the in-between of light and dark, and the living and the dead. The ancient Gaels believed it as a time when the boundaries between the living and spiritual worlds grew thin.

Queer people know thresholds intimately. Many queer lives involve standing between categories of genders, between the closet and the open, between safety and danger, between freedom and criminalisation, between the family of origin and the chosen family. Mainstream Western culture often treats that in-between place as undesirable, and being in it as a problem to fix. Samhain treats it as sacred. On this night, the space in-between is not a failure to belong but the very place to embrace, where mystery, insight and transformation happen.

Across many cultures and eras, people who did not fit neatly into binary gender categories were perceived as higher spiritual beings and healers. These traditions vary widely in different communities but they acknowledge that embracing the in-between and the edges of human experience can represent a holy space.

Reclaiming the witch

The witch is one of Halloween's most prominent figures. For centuries the witch was a symbol of societal fear: the woman outside male control, the healer outside the church, the person who refused to conform. Those accused of witchcraft were often people on the margins. It is not surprising that many queer people intimately associate with her.

Modern paganism and Wicca offer queer people spiritual paths that celebrate the body, pleasure and nature, rather than condemning them. Some of these traditions were shaped by queer and feminist practitioners from the start, blending pagan rituals with queer liberation. Many covens and circles now centre trans, non-binary and queer/LGBTQ+ members explicitly.

In these communities, Samhain is often the most important festival of the year, sometimes described as the witches' new year. To celebrate it as a queer person can honour a figure once used to persecute outsiders, and reclaiming our right to the sacred.

Queer ancestors

Honouring ancestors lies at the heart of festivals like Samhain, All Souls' Day and Día de Los Muertos. But for many queer people, it can be complicated. Blood relatives do not always accept queer people and sometimes shun them. Queer people can be erased from their own family trees.

However, Queer Spirituality widens the idea of lineage. Our ancestors can include the activists who fought for our rights—at Stonewall, for example, and at countless other protests worldwide. We can honour the gay and queer writers and artists who represented us in various ways, making our lives seen and heard. We can remember the people lost to the AIDS crisis. Ancestors can include the unnamed gay and queer people of every century, whose stories were never written down. They can include the friends, mentors and allies who welcomed us into community.

On Samhain, some queer people build altars to this chosen lineage, with photographs, books, candles and objects that carry memory. Speaking the names of our gay and queer people out loud is an act of love, remembrance and resistance. It says that these lives mattered, we stand on their shoulders, and we stand together.

Facing The Shadow

Samhain/Halloween invites us to look at The Shadow: what frightens us, and the parts of ourselves that are hidden or denied or that we have been taught to fear.

For many queer people, The Shadow holds internalised shame—the messages absorbed in childhood, and on an ongoing basis, that we are bad or wrong. Samhain/Halloween offers a symbolic container for shame with love and compassion rather than avoidance and self-harm. Rituals of release, such as writing down an old negative belief and burning it, can mark a commitment to ourselves to let go of what is not actually true about ourselves. Of course these rituals do not replace therapy but they can be practiced as part of the therapeutic and spiritual journey.

Celebrating the night

You don’t need to belong to any specific tradition to celebrate Samhain/Halloween meaningfully. A few simple practices can be enough to connect with your queer spirituality, such as:

  • Lighting a candle for a queer ancestor and speaking their name.
  • Creating a small altar with photographs or objects that honour your chosen lineage.
  • Writing down a fear or old negative belief you are ready to release, then safely burning it.
  • Sharing a meal with chosen family and telling stories of those who came before.
  • Taking a quiet walk at dusk and noticing the turning of the year.

Halloween has always been a festival for those who live on the edges. For queer people seeking the sacred, it offers something many religions withhold: a night when difference is holy, when the outsider is honoured, and when the dead and the living gather as one family. In the thin boundary between the living and spiritual worlds, many queer people find their sacredness, and themselves.
